Almost every clinical paper starts with **Table 1**: who was studied. Reviewers read it first, to decide whether your patients look like theirs and whether your groups were comparable to begin with. This page builds one from scratch.

::: {.callout-note .page-brief}
## 🎯 Goals and time
**After this page you can:**

- Make a Table 1 that compares two groups in R or Python, with mean (SD), median (IQR) or n (%) as each variable needs, and read off which characteristic differs most by its standardized mean difference (SMD).
- Choose between p-values and SMDs for a baseline table, from how the groups were formed.
- Write the first sentence of a Results section that describes a cohort.

**Time:** about 20 minutes to read, about 1 to 1.25 hours with the exercises (an estimate).

**Read first:** [How results are reported](../getting-started/using-this-site.qmd#how-results-are-reported), for the reporting conventions that Exercise 3 uses.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## 💡 In plain language
Table 1 *describes* your patients. It doesn't answer your research question. Its job is to let a reader judge who your results apply to, and whether your groups started out alike.
:::

## Load the data and pick the variables {#setup}

We'll describe the practice [cohort](../glossary.qmd#cohort){.term}: 600 primary hip and knee replacements (THA and TKA). Table 1 usually holds the characteristics measured *before* surgery. Length of stay is an outcome, measured after surgery: it is in this page's tables only as the example of a skewed variable, and where the tables compare groups, its row is not read as a sign of how alike the groups were before surgery.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R

```{r}
#| warning: false
library(tidyverse)
library(gtsummary)

cohort <- read_csv("data/cohort.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(asa = factor(asa))   # ASA class is a category, not a number

table1_vars <- c("age", "sex", "bmi", "asa", "diabetes", "smoker", "los_days")

labels <- list(age ~ "Age, years", sex ~ "Sex", bmi ~ "BMI, kg/m²", asa ~ "ASA class",
               diabetes ~ "Diabetes", smoker ~ "Smoking status",
               los_days ~ "Length of stay, days")

nrow(cohort)                                  # rows: one per procedure
cohort |>
  count(patient_id, name = "procedures") |>   # how many procedures each patient had
  count(procedures, name = "patients")        # how many patients had 1 procedure, how many had 2
```

## Python

```{python}
import pandas as pd
from tableone import TableOne

cohort = pd.read_csv("data/cohort.csv")
cohort["asa"] = cohort["asa"].astype(str)   # ASA class is a category, not a number

table1_vars = ["age", "sex", "bmi", "asa", "diabetes", "smoker", "los_days"]
categorical = ["sex", "asa", "diabetes", "smoker"]

labels = {"age": "Age, years", "sex": "Sex", "bmi": "BMI, kg/m²", "asa": "ASA class",
          "diabetes": "Diabetes", "smoker": "Smoking status",
          "los_days": "Length of stay, days"}

print(len(cohort))                                    # rows: one per procedure
per_patient = cohort["patient_id"].value_counts()     # how many procedures each patient had
# how many patients had 1 procedure, how many had 2
print(per_patient.value_counts().rename_axis("procedures").rename("patients"))
```
:::

```{python}
#| include: false
chk = {"rows": float(len(cohort)), "one": float((per_patient == 1).sum()), "two": float((per_patient == 2).sum())}
```

```{r}
#| include: false
check_agree(list(rows = nrow(cohort), one = sum(table(cohort$patient_id) == 1), two = sum(table(cohort$patient_id) == 2)),
            reticulate::py$chk)
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## ⚠️ Watch out: one row per procedure, not per patient
The cohort has one row per *procedure*. The count above shows 440 patients with one procedure and 80 with two (both sides): 440 + 80 = 520 patients, and 440 + 2 × 80 = 600 procedures. Say which one your table counts, for example in a footnote: "600 procedures in 520 patients". The two procedures of a bilateral patient are not [independent](../glossary.qmd#independence){.term} (same person, same age, sex and health), so tests that treat every row as a separate patient are slightly overconfident. [Distributions & choosing a test](03-distributions.qmd#paired) explains the options.
:::

## One group {#one-group}

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R

```{r}
table_one <- cohort |>
  select(all_of(table1_vars)) |>
  tbl_summary(
    type      = list(los_days ~ "continuous"),          # few distinct values, but still a number
    statistic = list(all_continuous() ~ "{mean} ({sd})",
                     los_days ~ "{median} ({p25}–{p75})"),
    digits    = list(all_continuous() ~ 1, los_days ~ 0),   # 65.5 (9.4); whole days
    label     = labels
  )
table_one
```

## Python

```{python}
table_one = TableOne(
    cohort,
    columns=table1_vars,
    categorical=categorical,
    nonnormal=["los_days"],      # report median [Q1, Q3] instead of mean (SD)
    rename=labels,
)
print(table_one.tabulate(tablefmt="github"))
```
:::

```{python}
#| include: false
chk = {"n": float(len(cohort)), "mean_age": float(cohort["age"].mean()),
       "sd_age": float(cohort["age"].std()), "female": float((cohort["sex"] == "Female").sum()),
       "median_los": float(cohort["los_days"].median())}
```

```{r}
#| include: false
check_agree(list(n = nrow(cohort), mean_age = mean(cohort$age), sd_age = sd(cohort$age),
                 female = sum(cohort$sex == "Female"), median_los = median(cohort$los_days)),
            reticulate::py$chk)
```

What happens if you don't tell it? Here is each package left to guess, on one [variable](../glossary.qmd#variable){.term}:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R

```{r}
cohort |> select(los_days) |> tbl_summary()   # no type given: length of stay is listed as a category
```

## Python

```{python}
print(TableOne(pd.read_csv("data/cohort.csv"), columns=["asa"]).tabulate(tablefmt="github"))   # no categorical list: ASA class is averaged
```
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## ⚠️ Watch out: tell the software what each variable is
Software guesses variable types, and the guesses are often wrong:

- **ASA class** looks like a number, so tableone averages it unless you list it under `categorical`: "mean (SD) 2.4 (0.7)" in the Python output above. It's a [category](../glossary.qmd#categorical-variable){.term}.
- **Length of stay** has only a few distinct values, so gtsummary treats it as a category and lists a row for 0, 1, 2 … days, as in the R output above. It's a count.
- **0/1 columns** such as `diabetes`: gtsummary shows a single row (how many are 1, i.e. yes), while tableone shows both the 0 and the 1 row. In a paper, show just the "yes" row.

Set the type of every variable yourself (`type =` in R, `categorical =` in Python).
:::

## Mean (SD) or median (IQR)? {#which-summary}

- **Roughly symmetric** continuous variables (age, BMI): [mean](../glossary.qmd#mean){.term} ([SD](../glossary.qmd#standard-deviation){.term}).
- **Skewed** variables, or variables **piled up at a [floor or ceiling](../glossary.qmd#ceiling-effect){.term}** (length of stay; often a [PROM](../glossary.qmd#prom){.term} 1 year after surgery): [median](../glossary.qmd#median){.term} ([IQR](../glossary.qmd#iqr){.term}). One patient with a 30-day stay drags the mean far more than the median.
- **Categories**: n (%).

How do you know whether a [variable](../glossary.qmd#variable){.term} is [skewed](../glossary.qmd#skewed){.term}? Look at it: [Distributions & choosing a test](03-distributions.qmd) shows how. Length of stay is strongly right-skewed, which is why it gets a median.

::: {.callout-tip}
## 🔀 R vs Python: quartiles
gtsummary and tableone use different formulas for [quartiles](../glossary.qmd#quartile){.term} (in R's terms, `quantile()` types 2 and 7). With whole-number data like length of stay the results can differ. In the table above the two agree (0 to 1 day). In the THA column of the [next table](#by-group) they don't: the upper quartile is 2 days in R (`1 (0–2)`) and 1.8 in Python (`1.0 [0.0,1.8]`). Neither is wrong. Say in your Methods which software you used.
:::

## Comparing groups {#by-group}

Most studies compare groups. Here: THA vs TKA.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R

```{r}
by_procedure <- cohort |>
  select(procedure, all_of(table1_vars)) |>
  tbl_summary(
    by        = procedure,
    type      = list(los_days ~ "continuous"),
    statistic = list(all_continuous() ~ "{mean} ({sd})",
                     los_days ~ "{median} ({p25}–{p75})"),
    digits    = list(all_continuous() ~ 1, los_days ~ 0),
    label     = labels
  ) |>
  add_overall() |>
  add_p(test = list(all_continuous() ~ "t.test",        # Welch's t test
                    los_days ~ "kruskal.test",           # rank-based, for the skewed variable
                    all_categorical() ~ "chisq.test"),   # chi-square
        pvalue_fun = label_style_pvalue(digits = 3))     # p to three decimals
by_procedure
```

## Python

```{python}
by_procedure = TableOne(
    cohort,
    columns=table1_vars,
    categorical=categorical,
    nonnormal=["los_days"],
    groupby="procedure",
    pval=True,               # Welch's t test, Kruskal-Wallis, chi-square
    htest_name=True,         # show which test produced each p-value
    rename=labels,
)
print(by_procedure.tabulate(tablefmt="github"))
```
:::

```{python}
#| include: false
p_values = by_procedure.htest_table["P-Value"]
chk = {v: float(p_values[v]) for v in table1_vars}
```

```{r}
#| include: false
p_r <- by_procedure$table_body |> filter(row_type == "label")
check_agree(as.list(setNames(p_r$p.value, p_r$variable)), reticulate::py$chk)
```

Each [p-value](../glossary.qmd#p-value){.term} comes from a test you'll meet in the catalog: [Welch's t test](../catalog/06-two-unpaired-groups.qmd#unpaired-t) for the [symmetric](../glossary.qmd#symmetric){.term} [continuous variables](../glossary.qmd#continuous-variable){.term}, a [rank-based test](../catalog/06-two-unpaired-groups.qmd#mann-whitney) for length of stay ([Kruskal-Wallis](../glossary.qmd#kruskal-wallis-test){.term} with two groups is the [Mann-Whitney test](../glossary.qmd#mann-whitney-test){.term}), and the [chi-square test](../catalog/06-two-unpaired-groups.qmd#fisher-chi-square) for the [categories](../glossary.qmd#categorical-variable){.term}. For diabetes R prints `>0.999` and Python `1.000`. It is the same p-value: tableone rounds it to three decimals. Report it as p > 0.999, as this site's conventions do.

ASA class has an order (1 to 4), and the chi-square test ignores the order: it treats the classes as unordered categories. That is acceptable here, where the aim is to describe the groups; to compare an ordered outcome between groups, use a rank-based test ([page 3](03-distributions.qmd#ordinal)). Each test also counts all 600 rows as separate patients, although the rows include both procedures of the 80 bilateral patients (the [warning](#setup) at the top of the page). The next section shows what that does to one p-value.

## p-values or standardized mean differences? {#smd}

Look at sex in the table above: 66% of THA procedures are in women against 50% of TKA procedures, p < 0.001. Is that a real difference between hip and knee patients?

In this practice dataset we know the answer, because we wrote the program that made it: sex was drawn **completely independently** of procedure. The difference is chance, and a rare fluke of this particular random draw. (In real arthroplasty [cohorts](../glossary.qmd#cohort){.term}, TKA patients are usually *more* often female.)

Part of the small p-value comes from counting the 80 bilateral patients twice. Run the same test with one row per patient, keeping each patient's first procedure:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R

```{r}
patients <- cohort |> distinct(patient_id, .keep_all = TRUE)   # one row per patient: the first procedure
nrow(patients)

sex_test <- chisq.test(table(patients$sex, patients$procedure),
                       correct = TRUE)   # Yates' continuity correction, as in the table above
sex_test
```

## Python

```{python}
from scipy import stats

patients = cohort.drop_duplicates("patient_id")   # one row per patient: the first procedure
print(len(patients))

sex_test = stats.chi2_contingency(pd.crosstab(patients["sex"], patients["procedure"]),
                                  correction=True)   # Yates' continuity correction, as in the table above
print(sex_test.pvalue)
```
:::

```{python}
#| include: false
chk = {"patients": float(len(patients)), "p": float(sex_test.pvalue)}
```

```{r}
#| include: false
check_agree(list(patients = nrow(patients), p = sex_test$p.value), reticulate::py$chk)
```

p = 0.002 for the 520 patients, against p < 0.001 for the 600 procedures. Still small: chance does produce rare results, and across a long table of tests some turn up. That's the first problem with [p-values](../glossary.qmd#p-value){.term} in [Table 1](../glossary.qmd#table-1){.term}.

The second problem is that a p-value mixes up *how big* a difference is with *how many patients* you have. With 6,000 patients a trivial difference gets p < 0.001. With 30, a large one doesn't.

The **standardized mean difference (SMD)** measures only the size of the imbalance, in [standard-deviation](../glossary.qmd#standard-deviation){.term} units, whatever the [sample size](../glossary.qmd#sample-size){.term}. For a number such as age, it is the difference between the two groups' means divided by their pooled SD, the square root of the average of the two groups' [variances](../glossary.qmd#variance){.term}. For a variable with two categories, such as sex, the means are the two groups' proportions (here, the share of women), and the variance of a proportion p is p(1 − p). For sex, with 177 of the 270 THA procedures and 166 of the 330 TKA procedures in women (the counts in the tables above), this gives the 0.31 in the table below. The SMD is computed from these counts, not from the rounded percentages. For a variable with more than two categories, such as ASA class or smoking status, both packages combine the differences in all the categories into one distance between the groups, which is always positive.

A common rule of thumb: |SMD| below 0.1 is negligible. Treat it as a rough guide, not a line between "balanced" and "unbalanced": with a few hundred patients, chance alone can produce SMDs above it, even when the groups were formed at random. [Exercise 1](#exercises) shows this.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R

```{r}
balance <- cohort |>
  select(procedure, all_of(table1_vars)) |>
  tbl_summary(
    by        = procedure,
    type      = list(los_days ~ "continuous"),
    statistic = list(all_continuous() ~ "{mean} ({sd})",
                     los_days ~ "{median} ({p25}–{p75})"),
    digits    = list(all_continuous() ~ 1, los_days ~ 0),
    label     = labels
  ) |>
  add_difference(test = everything() ~ "smd")
balance
```

## Python

```{python}
balance = TableOne(
    cohort,
    columns=table1_vars,
    categorical=categorical,
    nonnormal=["los_days"],
    groupby="procedure",
    smd=True,
    rename=labels,
)
print(balance.smd_table)
```
:::

```{python}
#| include: false
smd = balance.smd_table.iloc[:, 0]
chk = {v: abs(float(smd[v])) for v in table1_vars}
```

```{r}
#| include: false
smd_r <- balance$table_body |> filter(row_type == "label")
# Continuous SMDs differ in the 3rd decimal (variance divided by n in R's smd
# package, n - 1 in tableone), documented in the R vs Python box below.
check_agree(as.list(setNames(abs(smd_r$estimate), smd_r$variable)), reticulate::py$chk, tol = 0.005)
```

Ignoring the signs for now (the box below explains them), sex (SMD 0.31) and BMI (0.33) are the clear imbalances. Age (0.10), ASA class (0.12) and smoking (0.15) are just over 0.1: worth a sentence, not alarm. Diabetes is negligible. The length-of-stay row is not read here: length of stay is an outcome, so its SMD says nothing about how alike the groups were before surgery. R's table also gives a 95% [CI](../glossary.qmd#confidence-interval){.term} for each SMD; tableone doesn't compute one.

The two packages agree to three decimals. To see where they part, print the age SMD with more digits:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R

```{r}
smd::smd(cohort$age, cohort$procedure)   # the function gtsummary calls; its table rounds this to 0.10
```

## Python

```{python}
print(round(abs(balance.smd_table.loc["age"].iloc[0]), 4))   # the age row of the table above, without its sign
```
:::

```{python}
#| include: false
chk = {"age": float(abs(balance.smd_table.loc["age"].iloc[0]))}
```

```{r}
#| include: false
# The two packages divide the variances differently (n against n - 1; see the box), so the
# continuous SMDs differ in the fourth decimal.
check_agree(list(age = abs(smd::smd(cohort$age, cohort$procedure)$estimate)), reticulate::py$chk, tol = 0.005)
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## 🔀 R vs Python: SMDs differ slightly
- **Sign.** For the [variables](../glossary.qmd#variable){.term} entered as numbers (age, BMI, length of stay), gtsummary subtracts TKA from THA and tableone subtracts THA from TKA, so the signs are opposite. For [categories](../glossary.qmd#categorical-variable){.term} (sex, ASA class, smoking) the SMD has no direction and is positive in both. Report the absolute value, or say which group was subtracted from which.
- **Fourth decimal.** For [continuous variables](../glossary.qmd#continuous-variable){.term}, R's `smd` package divides the variances by *n*, while tableone divides by *n − 1* (the usual textbook formula). Age comes out as 0.1048 in R and 0.1046 in Python (the two numbers printed just above the box). Categorical SMDs match exactly.
:::

**Which should you report?**

- **Randomized trials**: no p-values for baseline differences. In a randomized trial any baseline difference is due to chance by construction, so a p-value for it answers no question; the CONSORT guideline for reporting trials advises against such tests.
- **Matched or weighted cohorts** ([propensity-score](../glossary.qmd#propensity-score){.term} studies, such as a [matched](../glossary.qmd#matched){.term} study of patients over 80): SMDs only. The matching made the groups alike on purpose, so a test of "did they differ?" makes no sense.
- **Other observational comparisons**: many journals still expect p-values. Give SMDs alongside, and discuss differences by their size, not their p-value.

## Missing data {#missing}

The [tidy](../glossary.qmd#tidy-data){.term} version of the messy workbook from [page 1](01-tidy-data.qmd) is missing a few BMIs, ASA classes and lengths of stay. [Missing values](../glossary.qmd#missing-data){.term} must show up in [Table 1](../glossary.qmd#table-1){.term}. Never drop them silently.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R

```{r}
abstraction <- read_csv("data/answer-keys/abstraction_workbook_tidy.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(asa = factor(asa))

abstraction |>
  select(site, age, bmi, asa, los_days) |>
  tbl_summary(by = site, type = list(los_days ~ "continuous"),
              statistic = list(all_continuous() ~ "{mean} ({sd})",
                               los_days ~ "{median} ({p25}–{p75})"),
              digits = list(all_continuous() ~ 1, los_days ~ 0),
              missing_text = "Missing")
```

## Python

```{python}
abstraction = pd.read_csv("data/answer-keys/abstraction_workbook_tidy.csv")
abstraction["asa"] = abstraction["asa"].astype("Int64").astype("string")   # a category; blanks stay missing

missing_table = TableOne(abstraction, columns=["age", "bmi", "asa", "los_days"],
                         categorical=["asa"], nonnormal=["los_days"],
                         groupby="site", missing=True,
                         include_null=False)   # count blanks as missing, not as a "None" category
print(missing_table.tabulate(tablefmt="github"))
```
:::

```{python}
#| include: false
chk = {"missing_bmi": float(abstraction["bmi"].isna().sum()),
       "missing_asa": float(abstraction["asa"].isna().sum())}
```

```{r}
#| include: false
check_agree(list(missing_bmi = sum(is.na(abstraction$bmi)),
                 missing_asa = sum(is.na(abstraction$asa))), reticulate::py$chk)
```

R adds a "Missing" row under each variable that has any, with one count per site (BMI: 5 and 3). Python adds a "Missing" column for both sites together (BMI: 8 = 5 + 3). Either way, the percentages are of the patients with a value: at Site A, 6 of the 58 patients with an ASA class are in class 1, which is 10.3% (Python's `6 (10.3)`), not 6 of 60. The reader can see how many were left out.

## Exporting to Word {#export}

Journals want [Table 1](../glossary.qmd#table-1){.term} in Word. Save it into your `scratch/` folder (git ignores it), open it, and paste it into the manuscript.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R

```{r}
by_procedure |>
  as_flex_table() |>
  flextable::save_as_docx(path = "scratch/table1.docx")
```

## Python

```{python}
from docx import Document

table = by_procedure.tableone.reset_index()
headers = [" ".join(str(part) for part in col if part).strip() for col in table.columns]

doc = Document()
grid = doc.add_table(rows=1, cols=len(headers))
for cell, header in zip(grid.rows[0].cells, headers):
    cell.text = header
for _, row in table.iterrows():
    for cell, value in zip(grid.add_row().cells, row):
        cell.text = "" if pd.isna(value) else str(value)
doc.save("scratch/table1-python.docx")
```
:::

In Word, tidy the formatting to the journal's style: usually no vertical lines, and a footnote that says which statistics are shown ("mean (SD); median (IQR); n (%)") and which tests produced the [p-values](../glossary.qmd#p-value){.term}.

::: {.callout-note .key-points}
## 📌 Key points
- The cohort has one row per procedure, not per patient: say which one your table counts, for example in a footnote ("600 procedures in 520 patients").
- Software guesses variable types, and the guesses are often wrong: set the type of every variable yourself.
- Summarize roughly symmetric continuous variables as mean (SD), skewed variables or variables piled up at a floor or ceiling as median (IQR), and categories as n (%).
- A p-value mixes up how big a difference is with how many patients you have; the SMD measures only the size of the imbalance, whatever the sample size.
- In a randomized trial, give no p-values for baseline differences; in a matched or weighted cohort, give only SMDs; in other observational comparisons, give SMDs alongside the p-values many journals still expect.
- Missing values must show up in Table 1: never drop them silently.
:::

```{r}
#| include: false
# Prose guard: numbers quoted in the text above. If the data change, update the text.
pct <- function(x) round(100 * mean(x))
site_table <- cohort |>
  select(site, all_of(table1_vars)) |>
  tbl_summary(by = site, type = list(los_days ~ "continuous")) |>
  add_difference(test = everything() ~ "smd")
site_rows <- site_table$table_body |> filter(row_type == "label")
site_smd <- setNames(abs(site_rows$estimate), site_rows$variable)
stopifnot(
  nrow(cohort) == 600, n_distinct(cohort$patient_id) == 520,
  sum(table(cohort$patient_id) == 1) == 440, 440 + 80 == 520, 440 + 2 * 80 == 600,
  sum(table(cohort$patient_id) == 2) == 80,
  sum(cohort$procedure == "THA") == 270, sum(cohort$procedure == "TKA") == 330,
  pct(cohort$sex[cohort$procedure == "THA"] == "Female") == 66,
  pct(cohort$sex[cohort$procedure == "TKA"] == "Female") == 50,
  round(mean(cohort$age), 1) == 65.5, round(sd(cohort$age), 1) == 9.4,
  sum(cohort$sex == "Female") == 343, pct(cohort$sex == "Female") == 57,
  median(cohort$los_days) == 1,
  # numbers added with the audit fixes
  round(smd::smd(cohort$age, cohort$procedure)$estimate, 4) == 0.1048,
  round(abs(reticulate::py_eval("float(balance.smd_table.loc['age'].iloc[0])")), 4) == 0.1046,
  round(mean(as.integer(as.character(cohort$asa))), 1) == 2.4, round(sd(as.integer(as.character(cohort$asa))), 1) == 0.7,
  sort(unique(cohort$los_days)) == 0:6,
  tapply(is.na(abstraction$bmi), abstraction$site, sum) == c(5, 3), 5 + 3 == 8,
  sum(!is.na(abstraction$asa[abstraction$site == "Site A"])) == 58,
  sum(abstraction$asa[abstraction$site == "Site A"] == 1, na.rm = TRUE) == 6, round(100 * 6 / 58, 1) == 10.3,
  # what the libraries actually display (Python side checked in the next chunk)
  by_procedure$table_body$stat_1[by_procedure$table_body$variable == "los_days" &
                                   by_procedure$table_body$row_type == "label"] == "1 (0–2)",
  by_procedure$table_body$stat_0[by_procedure$table_body$variable == "los_days" &
                                   by_procedure$table_body$row_type == "label"] == "1 (0–1)",
  by_procedure$table_body$stat_0[by_procedure$table_body$variable == "age" &
                                   by_procedure$table_body$row_type == "label"] == "65.5 (9.4)",
  round(abs(smd_r$estimate[smd_r$variable == "age"]), 2) == 0.10,
  round(abs(smd_r$estimate[smd_r$variable == "asa"]), 2) == 0.12,
  round(abs(smd_r$estimate[smd_r$variable == "smoker"]), 2) == 0.15,
  abs(smd_r$estimate[smd_r$variable == "diabetes"]) < 0.1,
  abs(smd_r$estimate[smd_r$variable == "los_days"]) < 0.1,
  abs(site_smd[["smoker"]] - 0.23) < 0.005, abs(site_smd[["los_days"]] - 0.225) < 0.005,
  all(site_smd[setdiff(names(site_smd), c("smoker", "los_days"))] < 0.11),
  round(abs(smd_r$estimate[smd_r$variable == "sex"]), 2) == 0.31,
  round(abs(smd_r$estimate[smd_r$variable == "bmi"]), 2) == 0.33,
  # numbers and claims added with the content-review fixes (B23, C11, C14)
  sum(cohort$sex == "Female" & cohort$procedure == "THA") == 177, sum(cohort$sex == "Female" & cohort$procedure == "TKA") == 166,
  nrow(patients) == 520, round(sex_test$p.value, 3) == 0.002, sex_test$p.value > 0.001,
  n_distinct(cohort$patient_id) == nrow(distinct(cohort, patient_id, sex, procedure)),   # sex, procedure: one per patient
  local({ p1 <- mean(cohort$sex[cohort$procedure == "THA"] == "Female"); p2 <- mean(cohort$sex[cohort$procedure == "TKA"] == "Female")
    isTRUE(all.equal(abs(smd_r$estimate[smd_r$variable == "sex"]), abs(p1 - p2) / sqrt((p1 * (1 - p1) + p2 * (1 - p2)) / 2))) }),
  all(smd_r$estimate[smd_r$variable %in% c("sex", "asa", "smoker")] > 0),
  reticulate::py_eval("all(balance.smd_table.iloc[:, 0][['sex', 'asa', 'smoker']] > 0)"),
  isTRUE(all.equal(chisq.test(table(cohort$asa, cohort$procedure))$p.value,
                   chisq.test(table(factor(cohort$asa, levels = c(3, 1, 4, 2)), cohort$procedure))$p.value)),   # order ignored
  site_smd[["smoker"]] > 0.1, round(site_smd[["asa"]], 2) == 0.10, site_smd[["asa"]] > 0.1,
  round(site_smd[["smoker"]], 2) == 0.23, round(site_smd[["los_days"]], 2) == 0.22,
  round(site_rows$conf.low[site_rows$variable == "smoker"], 2) == 0.07, round(site_rows$conf.high[site_rows$variable == "smoker"], 2) == 0.39,
  sum(names(site_smd) != "los_days") == 6
)
```

## Exercises {#exercises}

**1.** Make a [Table 1](../glossary.qmd#table-1){.term} comparing **Site A with Site B** instead of THA with TKA. Which [variable](../glossary.qmd#variable){.term} differs most between sites, by [SMD](../glossary.qmd#smd){.term}?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R

```{r}
cohort |>
  select(site, all_of(table1_vars)) |>
  tbl_summary(by = site, type = list(los_days ~ "continuous"),
              statistic = list(all_continuous() ~ "{mean} ({sd})",
                               los_days ~ "{median} ({p25}–{p75})"),
              digits = list(all_continuous() ~ 1, los_days ~ 0),
              label = labels) |>
  add_difference(test = everything() ~ "smd")
```

## Python

```{python}
by_site = TableOne(cohort, columns=table1_vars, categorical=categorical,
                   nonnormal=["los_days"], groupby="site", smd=True, rename=labels)
print(by_site.smd_table)
```
:::

Smoking status (0.23) is the baseline characteristic that differs most between sites. In R's table its 95% [CI](../glossary.qmd#confidence-interval){.term} (0.07 to 0.39) excludes zero; tableone gives no CI. ASA class is just over 0.1 as well (R prints 0.10, Python 0.103498). Yet site was assigned completely at random in this dataset, independent of everything else. With six baseline characteristics, a chance imbalance or two above 0.1 is to be expected: judge each SMD by its size and by whether it could plausibly matter, not by whether it is "[significant](../glossary.qmd#statistical-significance){.term}".

Length of stay also has an SMD above 0.1 (0.22; Python prints −0.22, see the box on signs), but it is an outcome, measured after surgery, so it plays no part in judging how alike the sites' patients were before surgery. (The program that made the data gives site no effect on length of stay, so this difference is chance too.)
:::

**2.** A fellow is comparing patients aged 80 or older with younger patients, [matched](../glossary.qmd#matched){.term} on sex, BMI and ASA class. Should the [baseline](../glossary.qmd#baseline){.term} table show [p-values](../glossary.qmd#p-value){.term} or SMDs? Why?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
SMDs. The matching was designed to make the groups alike, so testing whether they differ answers a question nobody asked, and with matched data the p-value mostly reflects [sample size](../glossary.qmd#sample-size){.term}. SMDs show how well the matching worked: aim for |SMD| below 0.1 on every matching variable.
:::

**3.** Write the first sentence of the Results describing this [cohort](../glossary.qmd#cohort){.term}, using the reporting conventions from [How to use this site](../getting-started/using-this-site.qmd).

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
"We included 600 primary arthroplasties (270 THA and 330 TKA) in 520 patients. Mean age was 65.5 (SD 9.4) years and 343 procedures (57%) were in women. Median length of stay was 1 (IQR 0 to 1) day."

Check every number against your own table: [mean](../glossary.qmd#mean){.term} and [SD](../glossary.qmd#standard-deviation){.term} for age, n (%) for sex, [median](../glossary.qmd#median){.term} ([IQR](../glossary.qmd#iqr){.term}) for length of stay. The 520 patients come from the count in [the first step](#setup).
:::
